title: Joshua 24:1–13
context: Joshua gathers all the tribes at Shechem, where they present themselves before God, and he speaks for the LORD, rehearsing Israel’s history from Terah’s household beyond the River, through Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Esau, the exodus, the Amorites east of the Jordan, Balak and Balaam, Jericho, and the conquest. The speech stresses that the LORD did all this and gave Israel a land they had not labored for. Both traditions read this recital as shared ground on grace: God’s prior acts are the basis of the covenant call that follows.

verses.text: Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem, and called for the elders of Israel, for their heads, for their judges, and for their officers; and they presented themselves before God.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua gathers all the tribes at Shechem, and they present themselves before God. Arminian readers note the significance of Shechem, where God first promised the land to Abraham (Gen 12:6–7).

The gathering is a covenant assembly, not just a farewell.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see Shechem’s history, including Jacob’s burial of foreign gods there (Gen 35:4).

Presenting themselves “before God” marks the meeting as an act of worship and covenant renewal.

verses.text: Joshua said to all the people, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘Your fathers lived of old time beyond the River, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nahor. They served other gods.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Israel’s fathers, including Terah, lived beyond the River and served other gods. Arminian readers note the honesty of the account: Israel’s story begins in idolatry (cf. Gen 11:26–31).

God’s call came to people who did not seek him first.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see sovereign grace in God’s calling of Abraham from an idolatrous family.

The River is usually understood as the Euphrates. Both traditions agree that Israel’s origin was God’s initiative, not its own merit.

verses.text: I took your father Abraham from beyond the River, and led him throughout all the land of Canaan, and multiplied his offspring, and gave him Isaac.
verses.arminianNotes:
God took Abraham from beyond the River, led him through Canaan, multiplied his offspring, and gave him Isaac. Arminian readers note the series of divine verbs: God takes, leads, multiplies, and gives.

“Offspring” can also be rendered “seed.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s initiative in every step of Abraham’s story (Gen 12:1–3).

The gift of Isaac, the child of promise, shows God working beyond natural possibility.

verses.text: I gave to Isaac Jacob and Esau: and I gave to Esau Mount Seir, to possess it. Jacob and his children went down into Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes:
God gave Isaac Jacob and Esau, gave Esau Mount Seir, and Jacob’s family went down to Egypt. Arminian readers note that Esau also receives a land from God (Gen 36:8; Deut 2:5).

God’s care extends beyond the chosen line.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God directing the histories of both brothers. Esau receives Seir, while the line of promise goes through Jacob.

The descent into Egypt is part of God’s plan, not a detour from it (Gen 46:3–4).

verses.text: “ ‘I sent Moses and Aaron, and I plagued Egypt, according to that which I did among them: and afterward I brought you out.
verses.arminianNotes:
God sent Moses and Aaron, plagued Egypt, and brought Israel out. Arminian readers note the brief summary of the exodus (Exod 3–12).

The “I” of God dominates the speech.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the exodus as God’s mighty redemption.

The divine first person stresses that deliverance was God’s act alone, which Israel can only receive.

verses.text: I brought your fathers out of Egypt: and you came to the sea. The Egyptians pursued your fathers with chariots and with horsemen to the Red Sea.
verses.arminianNotes:
God brought the fathers out, and the Egyptians pursued them to the Red Sea with chariots and horsemen. Arminian readers note the danger Israel faced.

The story builds toward God’s rescue at the sea.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the threat as setting the stage for God’s deliverance.

The present generation is addressed as if they were there, uniting them with their fathers’ experience of grace.

verses.text: When they cried out to the LORD, he put darkness between you and the Egyptians, and brought the sea on them, and covered them; and your eyes saw what I did in Egypt. You lived in the wilderness many days.
verses.arminianNotes:
When they cried to the LORD, he put darkness between them and the Egyptians and covered the Egyptians with the sea. Arminian readers note that God answered the people’s cry (Exod 14:10).

The wilderness years follow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s protecting presence (cf. Exod 14:19–20) and his judgment on Egypt.

“Your eyes saw what I did” makes the people witnesses of God’s saving power.

verses.text: “ ‘I brought you into the land of the Amorites, that lived beyond the Jordan. They fought with you, and I gave them into your hand. You possessed their land, and I destroyed them from before you.
verses.arminianNotes:
God brought Israel into the land of the Amorites east of the Jordan and gave them into their hand. Arminian readers recall the victories over Sihon and Og (Num 21:21–35).

The victories are God’s gift.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see Numbers 21. God destroyed the Amorites before Israel.

The pattern of divine action continues: God fights, and Israel possesses.

verses.text: Then Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and fought against Israel. He sent and called Balaam the son of Beor to curse you,
verses.arminianNotes:
Balak of Moab hired Balaam to curse Israel. Arminian readers note the reference to Numbers 22–24.

The phrase “fought against Israel” may refer to Balak’s hostile intent; Numbers does not record a battle with him, and interpreters discuss the wording.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the attempt to curse God’s people.

The verse sets up God’s refusal to listen to Balaam in the next verse.

verses.text: but I would not listen to Balaam; therefore he blessed you still. So I delivered you out of his hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
God would not listen to Balaam, so Balaam blessed Israel, and God delivered them. Arminian readers note that God turned the intended curse into blessing (Deut 23:5).

No human scheme can override God’s purpose.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty over even a hostile prophet’s words.

The Balaam story shows that God’s blessing on his people cannot be reversed by their enemies.

verses.text: “ ‘You went over the Jordan, and came to Jericho. The men of Jericho fought against you, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite; and I delivered them into your hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho, where the inhabitants and the seven nations fought them, and God delivered them. Arminian readers note the summary of the conquest (Josh 6–12).

The list of nations recalls the promise to Abraham.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness to the promise of the land.

The repeated “I delivered” attributes the conquest to God.

verses.text: I sent the hornet before you, which drove them out from before you, even the two kings of the Amorites; not with your sword, nor with your bow.
verses.arminianNotes:
God sent the hornet before them, which drove out the two Amorite kings, not by sword or bow. Arminian readers note the emphasis that victory was not by Israel’s weapons.

Whether the hornet is literal or a figure for panic or another means is debated (cf. Exod 23:28; Deut 7:20).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also stress “not with your sword, nor with your bow.”

The meaning of the hornet is debated, and ancient versions differ on the number of kings. The point is clear: God won the victory.

verses.text: I gave you a land on which you had not labored, and cities which you didn’t build, and you live in them. You eat of vineyards and olive groves which you didn’t plant.’
verses.arminianNotes:
God gave them land they had not worked for, cities they had not built, and vineyards and olive groves they had not planted. Arminian readers note the echo of Deuteronomy 6:10–11.

Israel lives in what it received as a gift.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a vivid picture of grace: receiving what one did not earn.

Both traditions agree that this recital of grace is the foundation for the call to serve the LORD that follows.
